title: What Time Do Morning Exercisers Go to Bed? Usually Before 10 | Terra
summary: We analyzed the routines of 192,000 people. In bed by 9pm, about one day in three has a morning workout; in bed at 2am, one in twenty, and the evening doesn’t…
body_markdown:
## When do people sleep


Figure 1 shows when each group is asleep. Each row is a bedtime slot, each column is an hour of the day, and dark blue means almost everyone in that box was asleep.


**Figure 1. Sleep slides later as the usual bedtime does.**


A bedtime label is the line beside the box, and the box is the half hour between that line and the next. The clock labels along the top and the bottom are the edges of each hour.


Read it from the top. People in the 9 pm slot tend to be up before 6 am. Move down the chart, and the sleep band slides to the right. The 1 am slot wakes around 8.30 am and sleeps about six and a half hours. Wake-up time moves much less than sleep time, which means shorter sleeps for people who go to bed late.


## What happens to activity


Figure 2 uses the same grid with a different question. Was there a recorded workout touching that hour?


A workout here is an activity with a start and an end, lasting from ten minutes to six hours. It counts in an hour if any part of it touches that hour. A run from 7.10 to 7.40 marks the 7.00 column. A longer one can mark two columns.


I used this method, because it shows both when the workout starts and also activity length.


**Figure 2. Morning workouts fade as bedtime gets later.**


Same lines and boxes as Figure 1. Colour is the share of tracked nights with a recorded workout touching that hour. August–October 2026.


In the early rows, for the early sleepers, the darkest cells sit at 6, 7 and 8 am. In the 8 pm slot that morning peak is about 18 percent of nights. As we follow the same columns down the colour lightens and then disappears!


The most interesting finding here is that the increased evening activity (of late sleepers) does not make up for the lack of morning activity. Between 5 and 9 pm, the share of nights with a workout moves from about 15 percent in the 9 pm sleepers slot to about 19 percent in the midnight sleepers slot, and then it stops climbing. Any workout at all, at any hour, falls from about 49 per cent of nights to about 34 percent. People who go to bed later are not swapping a morning session for an evening one. They do a bit less, and when they do it it’s later.


## Why the line is before 10


**Figure 3. Morning exercise stays common if you are in bed before 10.**


The brown line is for morning workouts (6–10am). The grey line is a workout starting within four hours of waking.


The 9 pm sleepers slot holds about 32 per cent of nights with a workout in the 6–10 am window. Once the median falls in the 10 pm slot, the share is about 26 per cent, and from there the line is fairly straight: 19 per cent for 11 pm sleepers down to about 5 per cent for the 2.00 am sleepers. From the 9.30 pm sleepers slot to the midnight sleepers slot, that is about six and a half percentage points for each hour the median falls later. Across everyone, the fitted slope is about 5.6 percentage points per hour. So it turns out that midnight is not the magic number, it’s more like 10pm.


The grey line is a kind of control, because maybe someone can sleep well until 10 am and still exercise after waking. Someone still in bed at 8 am is clearly not training at 7 am. So the grey line asks the same question: how likely is it that someone went to bed at that time and worked out within 4 hours of waking up? The line turns in the same place, then falls more slowly: 34 per cent of nights in the 9 pm sleepers slot, 20 per cent for the midnight sleepers, 14 per cent in the 2 am sleepers. Later bedtimes come with less exercise even after the person is awake.


Usual bedtime Workout 6.00–10.00am Within 4 hours of waking Any workout that day


9.00pm 31.5% 34.3% 49.2%


10.00pm 25.8% 29.2% 46.1%


11.00pm 19.3% 24.5% 43.0%


Midnight 12.9% 20.2% 39.2%


1.00am 8.0% 16.9% 36.3%


2.00am 4.6% 14.1% 33.7%


**Table 1. Share of tracked nights with a workout, by usual bedtime.**


Each row is the half-hour slot that starts at that time. The columns are each person’s average across August, September, and October, not the morning after one night.


There is a clear practical problem here. Figure 1 shows that 1 am and 2 am sleepers mostly wake up before 9 am, and remember this is a median figure. So we can presume there is probably time pressure to get to work, or do something, which practically makes exercise harder. For me, this points to the original point of the research: what do healthy lifestyle habits look like in the data; those that prioritise healthy behaviours.
